## Methods

Materials and reagents
6-Methoxy-2-acetylnaphthalene (MA, ≥99.0%) was purchased from Aladdin Chemical Co., Ltd. 1,2,4,5-Tetracyanobenzene (TCNB, ≥98.0%) was obtained from TCI Chemicals. (S)-Naproxen (S-NAP, ≥99.5%), and (R)-naproxen (R-NAP, ≥99.0%) were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Triphenylphosphine (TPP, ≥99.0%), dichloromethane (DCM, HPLC grade), acetonitrile (ACN, HPLC grade), ethanol (≥99.7%), methanol (≥99.9%), n-propanol (≥99.5%), n-butanol (≥99.5%), and n-pentanol (≥99.5%) were obtained from Chuandong Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Propyl 4-hydroxybenzoate (PHBA-Pr, ≥98.0%) and aqueous ammonia solution (25–28 wt%) were purchased from Aladdin Chemical Co., Ltd.
All chemicals were used as received without further purification unless otherwise stated. Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ·cm) was used in all experiments.

Instruments
Ultraviolet-visible (UV) absorption spectra were obtained by the UH4150 UV-Vis-NIR spectrophotometer combined with the diffuse reflection mode of the integrating sphere (Hitachi, Japan). Steady-state photoluminescence (PL) spectra were recorded on the F-7100 fluorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi, Japan). PL lifetime was measured by the FLS1000 fluorescence spectrometer (Edinburgh Instruments, UK). Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were measured on the IRTracer-100 spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan). Raman spectra were collected on the LabRAM HR800 spectrometer with a 633 nm laser excitation source (Horiba Jobin-Yvon, France). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) measurements were made by the X'Pert3 Powder10300 (PANalytical, Holland). Enantiomer ratios were determined by HPLC (Chiralpak AS-H columns were purchased from Daicel Chemical Industries, LTD). All single-crystal X-ray diffraction data were collected on the XtaLAB Synergy, Dualflex, HyPix diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (=1.54184 Å). With Olex2, all the structures were solved using the SHELXS structure solution program using the intrinsic phasing method, and all the structures were refined with the SHELXIL refinement package using least-squares minimization. Photographs were taken by an iPhone 13 camera.

Preparation of single crystals
Single crystals of different configurations were obtained by gas phase diffusion method. In a typical experiment, equimolar amounts of S-NAP (9.2 mg) and TCNB (7.1 mg) were dispersed in 4 mL of CH3CN using ultrasound to obtain a yellow solution, and the solution was passed through with a 0.45 μm syringe filter and transferred into a glass vial. The glass vial was placed in a sealed glass vial containing 8 mL of water under ambient conditions for several days, and high-quality single crystals were obtained by mutual diffusion of good and poor solvents.

Data availability
Crystallographic data for MT1 and MT2 have been deposited with the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (CCDC) under deposition numbers CCDC 2490358 (MT1) and CCDC 2490348 (MT2). These data can be obtained free of charge from the CCDC. The data supporting the findings of this study are available within the Article, Supplementary Information, or Source Data file. Source data are provided for Figures. 2b-e; 3a-d; 4a, c; 5a–c; 7b-d; 8b, c, e-h and Supplementary Figures. S4-S9, S11, S13-S26, S29, S32, S34-S37, S40-S43, S45-S48 in the associated source data file. Source data are provided with this paper. The Data is available from the corresponding authors on request.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The paper “Visualizing Molecular Diffusion Direction and Processes in the Solid State via Dichromatic Fluorescent Cocrystalization Transformation” by P. F. Gao et al. reports an intermolecular charge transfer-mediated fluorescence strategy to visualize and regulate solid state molecular motion (SSMM) in binary cocrystal systems. The study is important and presents a notable advance in the visualization of more detailed information about SSMM. Besides, the selective and unidirectional diffusion phenomenon in SSMM can provide valuable insights for the design of novel sensing platforms. Moreover, this work leverages the unique interaction characteristics between TCNB and MA to enable the impurity analysis of MA, a key impurity in naproxen, without the need for pretreatment. Furthermore, by exploiting the differential interaction capabilities between various naproxen esterification derivatives and TCNB, it enables the real-time monitoring of the transesterification reactions. The findings advance the field, meeting the high standards for urgency and novelty set by Nature Communications. I recommend acceptance after the minor revisions listed below.
1) As illustrated in Scheme 1, MA and TCNB tend to form the MT2 complex via “co-precipitation from solution”. However, this process was not characterized and discussed in the subsequent main text. The corresponding experimental data for characterizing this process should be provided along with necessary discussions in manuscript.
2) This study mainly investigates the unique interactions between TCNB and MA during grinding at the solid state and precipitation from solution. Regarding S-NAP, however, only the interactions induced by grinding are discussed. It remains to be determined whether the complex co-precipitated from the solution of S-NAP and TCNB is distinct from that formed by grinding.
3) For better understanding the optical properties of MA/TCNB, the fluorescence lifetimes of MA, TCNB and MA/TCNB should be determined and discussed in the text.
4) In Figure 5b and 5c, the authors observed unidirectional diffusion from MA to TCNB over time at 25°C. I wonder whether the SSMM between MA and TCNB would still exhibit unidirectional diffusion from MA to TCNB at higher temperatures.
5) How is the cuvette placed in Figure 5c? Is it vertical or flat on the table during the observation experiment? I wonder whether the form of placement employed by the authors can eliminate the influence of gravity on the SSMM direction.
6) I wonder how the luminescence of the complex would behave with further increases in the proportion of TCNB, as shown in Figure 6a. The authors are suggested to make more discussions about it. And what is the TCNB proportion in Figure 6b?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript describes a fascinating approach to monitoring solid-state molecular diffusion via fluorescence signals based on intermolecular charge transfer (ICT). Using 6-methoxy-2-acetylnaphthalene (MA) and 1,2,4,5-tetracyanobenzene (TCNB) as a model platform, the authors reveal a significant disparity in diffusion rates between the electron donor (MA) and acceptor (TCNB) at their interface. Remarkably, the system exhibits unidirectional diffusion from MA to TCNB within a specific time frame. While the core concept is novel and promising, the presentation and mechanistic depth of the study can be significantly enhanced to better support the claims and improve readability. The following points are recommended for the authors' consideration:
1. I think that Scheme 1 needs for molecular-level illustration. The current Scheme 1 appears to focus on macroscopic phenomena. To better align with the article's theme of "monitoring solid-state molecular diffusion via dichroic fluorescence signals," it is highly recommended to redesign this scheme to illustrate the process at the molecular level. This should depict the interaction between MA and TCNB molecules, the resulting ICT effect, and how this ultimately leads to the observed macroscopic optical output.
2. The inclusion of S-NAP as a control in Figure 2, while intended to show specificity, currently complicates the figure and dilutes the focus on the key finding (the MA-TCNB complex). It is suggested that Figure 2 be dedicated to a compelling series of data that conclusively demonstrates the formation of the MA-TCNB intermolecular complex and the ICT phenomenon. Furthermore, the authors claim that S-NAP fails to interact with TCNB due to self-aggregation. However, could the ICT phenomenon be achieved by modulating the S-NAP/TCNB ratio to disrupt this self-aggregation? A brief discussion or experimental data addressing this point would significantly strengthen the authors' claim regarding specificity.
3. The FTIR and Raman spectra presented in Figure 2c and 2d show rather subtle peak shifts. The question remains whether this evidence is robust enough to firmly prove the interaction between MA and TCNB. To strengthen this claim, is it needed to include the results for the MT1 and MT2 cocrystals in these panels for a direct and convincing comparison?
4. To enhance the visual impact and readability, it would be highly effective to include intrinsic fluorescence images of pure MA and TCNB powders in the main text. Presenting these alongside the fluorescence data of the cocrystals and diffusion composites would dramatically highlight the striking optical changes and underscore the "interesting effect" of the work.
5. As shown in Figures 5 and S15-16, the spontaneous diffusion between unground MA and TCNB powders is a notable observation. Could the authors discuss the driving forces behind this phenomenon, and whether any special preprocessing was used? If not, what are the thermodynamic or kinetic driving factors of this diffusion process?
6. Given the stated significance of monitoring diffusion processes and rates in solid state, Figure 5 presents a key opportunity for quantification. It is recommended that the authors add quantitative analysis, such as establishing a relationship between fluorescence color/intensity parameters and the amount of molecular diffusion. This could potentially form the basis for a general quantitative methodology for measuring solid-state diffusion kinetics.

Reply: Thank you for your insightful questions regarding the spontaneous diffusion
phenomenon reported in our study. We confirm that no special pre‑treatment was applied to the
samples and all powders were used in their pristine state. The underlying driving forces for this
phenomenon are rooted in fundamental molecular dynamics. Specifically, molecules in any
solid substance undergo continuous thermal motion. When two powder particles establish
intimate contact, this thermal agitation induces minute relative displacements at their interface,

occurs via localized stochastic processes analogous to Brownian motion, operating at particle
contact points. Owing to surface roughness and lattice imperfections, molecules at these
interfaces can execute thermally activated “jumps” across short distances. Over extended time
scales, the cumulative effect of these random events gives rise to observable macroscopic
diffusion. Moreover, the relatively weak intermolecular interactions among MA molecules
lower the activation barrier for diffusion, thereby facilitating the unidirectional migration of
MA into TCNB-rich domains. According to the reviewer's suggestion, we supplemented the
unidirectional diffusion experiment of MA to TCNB at 75°C. As shown in Figure S26, the
diffusion process at 75°C is significantly accelerated compared to that at 25°C. This
acceleration is attributed to the substantial enhancement of thermal motion of MA’s
unidirectional diffusion into TCNB. This further demonstrates that the thermal motion of
molecules is the primary driving force of the spontaneous diffusion between unground MA and
TCNB powders.
